name: Dental implants

image.caption: Patient specific transalveolar dental implants - front view

lead: Dental implants replace missing teeth with a fixed, natural-looking result. A titanium or zirconia post is set in the jawbone and topped with a crown, bridge or denture, so a gap is filled with a tooth that looks and works like the original.

The post bonds to bone through osseointegration, then supports the prosthetic tooth after healing. Reported survival is about 93 to 98 percent at five years or more in healthy tissue. On looksmaxxing forums people also ask whether implants and bone grafts can thicken the jaw or build chin projection, but reference sources describe implants as tooth replacements and do not describe such effects.

paras: Placement is oral surgery done in stages, with healing time before the crown is fitted. Rough surfaces and coatings are designed to speed bone attachment. People plan implants around gaps, failing teeth and the final shape of the smile.

Complications include infection, loosening, fracture, nerve injury and peri-implantitis (bone loss around the implant), which are more likely with smoking, poor hygiene and diabetes. It is a surgical, hard-to-reverse treatment.

angle.text: Dental implants replace missing teeth with a fixed, natural-looking result: a titanium root is set in bone and a crown fitted on top. Forum posters also ask about thickening the jaw or building up a recessed chin with implants and grafts, but that use is not described in reference sources.

lead: A dental implant is a prosthetic fixture, most often made of titanium or zirconia, that is anchored in the jaw bone to support a crown, bridge or denture. Modern implants rely on osseointegration, a close bond between living bone and the implant surface [1][2]. For appearance, the point is to replace a missing tooth with one that sits in the smile line like a natural tooth, closing gaps and restoring the look of a full dental arch without relying on neighbouring teeth or a removable plate [1].

The technique grew out of work by the Swedish physician Per-Ingvar Branemark, who observed in the early 1950s that bone grew tightly onto titanium and who placed the first titanium dental implant in a human patient in 1965 [1][2][3]. Since the 1980s, implants have become a mainstream option, and in the United States the share of patients missing a tooth who had an implant rose from 0.7 percent in 1999 to 2000 to 5.7 percent in 2015 to 2016 [1].

In looksmaxxing forums, implants are discussed mostly as a way to fill gaps, and occasionally with the question of whether an implant plus bone grafting can thicken or reshape the jaw. Encyclopedic sources describe implants as tooth-replacement devices and do not describe them as changing facial or jaw shape [1][4][5].

Research on implants is extensive. A 2019 systematic review of contemporary implant systems reported a pooled 10-year implant-level survival of 96.4 percent [6], while reviews of long-term outcomes describe complications such as peri-implantitis, loosening of screws and abutments, and fractures over longer follow-up [1][7][8].
infobox: Commercially pure titanium (most common); zirconia ceramic [1]
Branemark System, now sold by Nobel Biocare [3]
About 21 percent of patients in a 2025 meta-analysis [7]

paras: The implant is placed first and a prosthesis is attached after healing. Indications listed include single-tooth replacement, implant-supported bridges, implant-supported overdentures for toothless jaws, orthodontic anchorage and retention of facial prostheses [1]. Single-tooth replacement is described as a first-line option, and fixed bridges supported by implants can span a few teeth or a full arch [1].

Surgery typically involves exposing bone, drilling progressively wider holes with cooling, placing the implant and later attaching an abutment and crown [1]. Planning uses clinical examination, models and CT scans with computer software, sometimes with a surgical guide, and flapless placement is an alternative to opening the gum [1]. Loading may be immediate, early (about 1 to 12 weeks) or delayed (over 3 months) [1]. Bone and gum can shrink after tooth extraction, which is why bone grafts or sinus lifts are sometimes used before placement [1][9].

Root-form screw implants are the most common type, and most implant bodies use commercially pure titanium, with titanium alloy mainly in abutments and screws [1]. Other designs include zygomatic implants, which are longer and anchor in the cheekbone for people with little upper-jaw bone; small-diameter or mini implants, which need less bone and are used for denture retention or orthodontic anchorage; and short implants for sites where grafting or a sinus lift would otherwise be needed [1].

Zirconia implants exist as one-piece and two-piece systems. A reference summary notes they may lower the risk of peri-implant disease but that long-term success data are limited [1]. Surface roughness and osteoconductive coatings are described as favouring bone anchoring and faster biological fixation [10], and a chemically modified rough titanium surface was reported to enhance bone apposition in a preclinical study [11]. Animal models have long been used to test implant biomaterials [12].

Archaeological finds attributed to ancient cultures include bamboo pegs in China and shell or metal replacements in Egypt and a Mayan site in Honduras [1]. Greenfield's implant system of 1913 is described as among the earliest documented successes, and in 1940 Bothe, Beaton and Davenport noted that titanium placed in an animal tended to fuse with bone [1][2]. In 1951 Gottlieb Leventhal reported tightening of titanium screws placed in rat femurs [2].

In 1952 Branemark studied blood flow in rabbit bone through a titanium observation chamber and found that the bone had integrated so completely that the chamber could not be removed; he went on to name the phenomenon osseointegration [2][3]. In 1965 he placed implants in Gosta Larsson, a man born with severe jaw deformities, who used them for more than 40 years [2][3]. Branemark became professor of anatomy at the University of Gothenburg in 1969 and founded the Branemark Osseointegration Center there in 1989; he died in 2014 [3].

In the mid-1970s Branemark partnered with the Swedish defence company Bofors to manufacture implants, a venture that later became Nobel Biocare [2]. A conference in Toronto in the early 1980s, supported by George Zarb, is generally regarded as the point at which the wider scientific community accepted the technique [2][3]. A 1986 review proposed success criteria that have been widely cited since [13].

A widely cited 1986 review proposed criteria for judging long-term success of implants [13]. A multi-centre prospective study of 2,359 non-submerged implants reported 8-year life table results [14]. A 2019 systematic review of 18 prospective studies of contemporary implants (roughened surfaces, solid screw designs) estimated 10-year implant survival at 96.4 percent, with a prediction interval of 91.5 to 99.4 percent [6].

Reported figures in a general reference include integration failure of 1 to 6 percent in the first six months and long-term success without complications of 52 to 76 percent at 16 to 20 years, with complications in up to 48 percent of cases [1]. Reviews also describe how design choices affect bone around the implant: a 2025 meta-analysis found no significant difference in marginal bone loss between screw-retained and cement-retained prostheses, and lower loss with nonsplinted implants and platform-switched abutments [15].

Because implants stand in for natural teeth, their visible result depends on the crown and on the gum around it. Trials in the front of the mouth have compared timing of placement, for example a multicentre randomised trial of placing an implant at the time of extraction versus 12 weeks later, which compared the need for bone augmentation, complications and aesthetic outcomes [16]. A five-year randomised trial compared a volume-stable collagen matrix with a connective tissue graft for augmenting soft tissue at implant sites [17].

After a tooth is extracted, the bone and gum in the socket remodel; a 12-month prospective study documented bone healing and soft tissue contour changes after single-tooth extraction [9]. Clinicians use ridge preservation and grafting in some cases to maintain contour before an implant, and trials have compared techniques for this [18][19]. Mid-face and jaw contour, by contrast, are not described in reference sources as outcomes of implant placement [1].

Implant treatment involves surgery, a prosthetic crown and several visits, and prices differ widely between countries. Dental work including implants, crowns and veneers is among the services sought by medical tourists, with Turkey, Hungary, Albania and Mexico named as destinations that attract patients on price [20]. A reference summary lists risks of treatment abroad such as variable follow-up care, legal and insurance gaps, and the difficulty of returning for complications [20].

Reported surgical complications include infection, bleeding and injury to nerves, sinuses or vessels, and failure to integrate is more likely with smoking or poor health [1]. For single crowns at five years, one summary lists screw or abutment loosening in about 12.7 percent and implant fracture of 0.14 percent [1].

Peri-implant mucositis is reversible inflammation, while peri-implantitis involves bone loss and can lead to implant removal. A 2017 consensus workshop defined these conditions [21]. A 2025 meta-analysis of 102 studies reported patient-level prevalence of 46 percent for mucositis and 21 percent for peri-implantitis [7], while a 2022 review of 57 studies reported 19.5 percent at patient level and 12.5 percent at implant level and noted that definitions strongly affect the figures [8]. Bisphosphonate-related exposed bone of the jaws has been described as a consideration in jaw procedures [22].

Patient factors have been studied. A 2021 meta-analysis of 292 publications found higher failure risk in smokers than non-smokers (odds ratio about 2.4) [23]. A 2024 meta-analysis of 27 studies found a higher failure risk in probable bruxers (odds ratio about 2.2) [24]. A review of contraindications discusses medical conditions and medications that bear on candidacy [25], and a placebo-controlled randomised trial examined whether antibiotic prophylaxis is needed in implant surgery [26].

Users on looksmax.org have asked whether a molar implant with bone grafting would thicken a jaw that is less dense on one side [4][5], whether jaw surgery can be done after implants [27], whether implants can improve a recessed chin [28], and whether implants damage the jaw [29]. The threads are questions, and implants are not described as altering jaw or chin shape. Jaw and chin changes in these communities are more usually discussed under other procedures such as genioplasty and orthognathic surgery.

Human studies of implants are extensive. Registered trials include a 39-year follow-up of the world's first single dental implants [30], a trial of marginal bone around implants with different surface treatments supporting mandibular overdentures [31], a randomised comparison of flap designs over three years [32], a study of implants in patients with Sjogren's syndrome [33], and a randomised trial of materials in full-arch prosthetics [34]. These studies address tooth replacement and bone levels, not facial appearance. Treatment of peri-implant disease and extraction-socket changes have also been examined [21][9].

Meta-analyses summarise outcomes across many trials: pooled 10-year survival [6], peri-implant disease prevalence and risk indicators [7][8], smoking [23] and bruxism [24]. A 2025 AO/AAP analysis of prosthetic design examined marginal bone loss across restoration types [15]. Randomised trials have also compared immediate with delayed placement [16], soft tissue grafts [17], a synthetic bone substitute combined with mesenchymal stem cells for atrophic ridges [18], and ridge preservation techniques [19].

claims.claim: An implant plus a bone graft can thicken a weaker jawbone.
Implants can improve a recessed chin.
Implants might interfere with later jaw surgery, or damage the jaw.
Smoking and clenching are a risk to implant longevity.

timeline.event: Greenfield's implant system shows early evidence of osseointegration [1].
Bothe, Beaton and Davenport observe titanium tending to fuse with bone in an animal [2].
Leventhal reports titanium screws tightening in rat femurs [2].
Branemark finds a titanium chamber integrated into rabbit bone and later names the effect osseointegration [2][3].
Branemark places his first titanium dental implant in a human patient, Gosta Larsson [2][3].
Branemark partners with Bofors, a venture that later became Nobel Biocare [2].
Start of a follow-up of the world's first single dental implants, later reported at 39 years [30]. Branemark's Toronto presentation of the same period brings wide recognition [3].
A review proposes criteria for long-term implant success [13].
Branemark founds the Branemark Osseointegration Center in Gothenburg [3].
World Workshop consensus classifies peri-implant diseases and conditions [21].
Meta-analysis reports 96.4 percent pooled 10-year implant survival [6].
AO/AAP meta-analyses report on peri-implant disease prevalence and prosthetic design [7][15].
